Looking at the seasonality breakdown for the upcoming week from @AlmanacTrader, editor of the Stock Trader’s Almanac & Almanac Investor Newsletter, the last week of October has historically closed the month on a firm note, and in midterm years Day 21 (Thursday) has been quite strong.

Monday is trading day 18. Over the past 31 years it has been one of the weaker days of the month, with the major indices down about 0.2–0.4%. Tuesday and Thursday have more than made up for it, each adding roughly 0.3–0.5%, while Wednesday has been about flat. Net, the week has gained about 0.5–0.65% for every major index, including the Russell 2000. That has left October up about 1.5–1.9% on average for the large-cap indices and about 0.5% for the Russell 2000.

Midterm years have been stronger again, led by small caps. The Russell 2000 has gained about 1.6%, the Nasdaq about 0.85%, the Russell 1000 about 0.75%, and the Dow and S&P about 0.5%. Some of that gap reflects which years are averaged: the Russell data only start with the 1982 midterm, while the Dow and S&P go back to 1950. The standout is Thursday, the best day of the week for every midterm line, adding about 0.65–0.85%. For the DJIA, S&P and Russell 1000, that one day has matched or exceeded the entire week’s gain. October has finished up about 3–4% in midterm years, compared with 1.5–1.9% for the large caps across all years.

That hands off to November, the start of what the Almanac calls the “Best Six Months” (November–April), and to the midterm election on Tuesday, November 3rd. Historically, midterms have been followed by strength. 

The S&P 500 has been higher one year after all 19 midterm elections since 1950, by about 15% on average according to a Motley Fool count, and by 16.6% according to BNY. Even after 1986, with the October 1987 crash in that window, the S&P finished about 1% higher.

So maybe pollsters aren’t irrelevant after all. Despite just an ~20% chance of victory according to Polymarket and Kalshi, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva came from behind to win Brazil’s presidential runoff on Sunday, taking 51.76% of the vote to 48.24% for Flávio Bolsonaro, per the Financial Times.

The polls though had called it a statistical dead heat. Datafolha’s final survey had the race tied at 50% each, and the average of final polls gave Bolsonaro a narrow 50.9% to 49.1% edge, per Newsweek. That’s well within the margin of error, and a long way from the roughly 4-to-1 odds prediction markets gave Bolsonaro.

It’s also a first. No first-round runner-up had won the presidency since Brazil restored elections in 1989, and Lula turned Bolsonaro’s 2.2 million-vote first-round lead into a 4.4 million-vote margin, per the FT.

Markets aren’t taking it well. The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF (EWZ) is down over 17% in overnight trading. Traders had piled into Brazilian assets on hopes that Bolsonaro would be more committed to cutting spending. Lula has promised a fiscal adjustment without saying how he’ll deliver it, and has made clear he won’t sacrifice his social agenda to satisfy markets. He’ll also face a more hostile Congress after conservative parties made sweeping gains in this month’s congressional elections, per the FT.

By later tonight you should have the winner of Brazil's hotly contested Presidential contest pitting Trump-aligned upstart Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, and 80-year-old President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

"Patricio Navia, a clinical professor of liberal studies at New York University, said that unless pollsters corrected whatever caused the miss, they are likely to repeat it on Sunday, which would favor Bolsonaro."

Couple of interesting things about the election process. First, voting is a requirement. Failure to vote results in a fine, so turnout is quite high.

Second, all voting is digital with what is considered a highly secure process that compiles results quickly meaning a winner should be announced within a few  hours after polls close at 5pm local time (4pm ET).

I mentioned in the Week Ahead two weeks ago regarding the McClellan Summation Index that “when it does rebound, rallies in the NYSE Composite are generally fairly powerful.”

I wanted more granular detail, so I ran it through Claude:

The Index bottomed near −1,190 on Oct 8, its deepest reading since October 2023, though well short of the 2018, 2020 and 2022 washouts. 

What stands out is how little price damage came with it. The NYSE Composite fell just 5.4% from its Aug 14 high, the smallest drop of the 13 sub-zero breadth washouts since 2018.

History is supportive, with caveats. After the seven prior turns from below −1,000, the NYSE was higher three and six months later in six of seven cases, with a median gain of 12.4% at both points. 

But three of those seven, in October 2018 and twice in 2022, were followed by a lower price low within six months.

A turn in breadth hasn’t always marked the bottom in price. Across all 12 prior sub-zero turns, the NYSE was higher a month later 11 times. But 11 sessions in, this rebound is one of the softest. 

The NYSE is up 1.3% since the Oct 8 turn, against a median of 4.9% at the same point after prior turns. The Summation Index has climbed about 475 points to −711, against a median of roughly 1,290. Only two prior turns started slower on price, October 2018 and June 2022, and both were followed by lower price lows. That said, this washout came with the least price damage of the 13 turns, so there was less ground to make up.

Always interesting Top 10 charts of the week from @C_Barraud has his thoughts on the selling by Japanese investors in global bonds "for five consecutive weeks, the longest selling streak in four years."

As he notes, "the consequences for global bond markets could be significant," with Japanese yields now trading above US equivalents once hedging costs are taken into account. "Japanese life insurers manage around $2.5 trillion in assets. Several are already planning to maintain or increase their purchases of domestic bonds so we could be looking at a gradual reallocation of capital over several years."

Given that backdrop, I had Claude do an analysis of how Japan's flows line up with US 10-year yields, using Bank of Japan data on Japanese net purchases of foreign securities, and its takeaways were consistent with the theory.

1. Japan flows do have a strong correlation with the change in 10-year yields. Comparing rolling 12-month net purchases to the 12-month change in the US 10Y results in a correlation of about −0.66 since 2014. That is consistent with Japanese selling driving yields. The 2013 taper tantrum and 2022 stand out.

2. Neither series, though, conclusively leads the other; the fit is tightest when both are measured over the same period. So while that's consistent with Japanese selling pushing yields up (which makes a lot of sense), it is equally consistent with sharp rises/drops in yields and hedging costs pushing/pulling Japanese investors out/in. In 2022, the cost of hedging dollars back into yen went from roughly 0.2% to over 4%, and Japan sold a record amount of foreign bonds.

3. Flows have little correlation with a given level of 10-year yields. The correlation between Japan's rolling 12-month net purchases and the US 10Y level is weak: about −0.14 since 1997 and −0.4 since 2014.

So it seems the reallocation risk is very real if higher Japanese yields pull flows back home.

MarketWatch: The chances of a stock-market rally into the year end are rising, according to UBS, and they suggest a trade for investors to make.

In a note published Monday, the Swiss bank says: "From late October on, we see rising odds of a more correlated rally in equities if 1) rates/ oil pressures abate, 2) U.S. midterm election risks do not realize, 3) AI narratives/demand are supportive, 4) earnings beats provide a tailwind, and 5) corporate buyback activity and announcements pick up." [Um, yeah?]

The biggest risk, judging by how options traders are pricing likely moves in the S&P 500 (SPX), is around the midterm election, as UBS's chart shows.

But the S&P 500 has historically rallied an average of 6% from the end of September to the end of December in midterm election years, and an average of 14% from end September to end March, according to UBS.

"We see rising odds of a broadening in the equity market rally if the above catalysts turn out largely positive. Rising equity markets associated with rising correlations has historically resulted in stronger returns," they say.

UBS says the trade to make is to buy out of the money (OTM) call options on the S&P 500. OTM call options have a strike price above the current S&P 500 level and are bullish bet on the index that have greater risk and potentially greater reward.
